## Probability Spaces

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Probability Space

A **probability space** is a triple $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ where
$\Omega$ is a set of “outcomes,” $\mathcal{F}$ is a set of “events,” and
$P : \mathcal{F} \to [0,1]$ is a function that assigns probabilities to events.

We assume that $\mathcal{F}$ is a $\sigma$-field (or $\sigma$-algebra), i.e.,
a (nonempty) collection of subsets of $\Omega$ that satisfy

i) if $A \in \mathcal{F}$ then $A^c \in \mathcal{F}$, and

ii) if $A_i \in \mathcal{F}$ is a countable sequence of sets then $\bigcup_i A_i \in \mathcal{F}$.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Measure

A **measure** is a nonnegative countably
additive set function; that is, a function $\mu : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{\infty\}$ with

i) $\mu(A) \ge \mu(\emptyset) = 0$ for all $A \in \mathcal{F}$, and

ii) if $A_i \in \mathcal{F}$ is a countable sequence of disjoint sets, then

    $$
    \mu\left(\bigcup_i A_i\right) = \sum_i \mu(A_i).
    $$

If $\mu(\Omega) = 1$, we call $\mu$ a **probability measure**. Probability
measures are usually denoted by $P$.

In general, a measure may take the value $\infty$, i.e.,

$$
\mu : \mathcal{F} \to [0,\infty].
$$

:::

::: {#thm-1 name="Properties of Measures"}

Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ (a $\sigma$-field).

i) **Monotonicity.** If $A \subset B$ then $\mu(A) \le \mu(B)$.

ii) **Subadditivity.** If $A \subset \bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty} A_m$ then

    $$
    \mu(A) \le \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_m).
    $$

iii) **Continuity from below.** If $A_i \uparrow A$ (i.e.,
     $A_1 \subset A_2 \subset \cdots$ and $\bigcup_i A_i = A$), then
     $\mu(A_i) \uparrow \mu(A)$.

iv) **Continuity from above.** If $A_i \downarrow A$ (i.e.,
    $A_1 \supset A_2 \supset \cdots$ and $\bigcap_i A_i = A$), with
    $\mu(A_1) < \infty$, then $\mu(A_i) \downarrow \mu(A)$.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Classification of Measures

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. The following classes are not mutually exclusive.

1. **Finite measure.** A measure $\mu$ is finite if $\mu(X)<\infty$.

   For example, Lebesgue measure on $[0,2]$ is finite, with total mass $2$.

2. **Probability measure.** A measure $\mu$ is a probability measure if $\mu(X)=1$.

   Thus, every probability measure is a finite measure. For example, Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ is a probability measure.

3. **$\sigma$-finite measure.** A measure $\mu$ is $\sigma$-finite if there exist
   measurable sets $E_1,E_2,\ldots$ such that

   $$
   \begin{gathered}
   X = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} E_n, \\
   \mu(E_n) < \infty \quad \text{for every } n.
   \end{gathered}
   $$

   For example, Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is $\sigma$-finite because

   $$
   \begin{gathered}
   \mathbb R = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} [-n,n], \\
   m([-n,n]) = 2n < \infty.
   \end{gathered}
   $$

4. **Infinite measure.** A measure $\mu$ is infinite if $\mu(X)=\infty$.

   An infinite measure may or may not be $\sigma$-finite. Counting measure on $\mathbb N$ is $\sigma$-finite, whereas counting measure on $\mathbb R$ is not.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Generated $\sigma$-Fields

If we are given a set $\Omega$ and a collection $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of $\Omega$, then there is a smallest $\sigma$-field containing $\mathcal{A}$. We call this the $\sigma$-field **generated by** $\mathcal{A}$ and denote it by $\sigma(\mathcal{A})$.

Let $\mathbb{R}^d$ be the set of vectors $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ of real numbers and $\mathcal{R}^d$ be the
**Borel sets**, the smallest $\sigma$-field containing the open sets. When $d=1$
we drop the superscript.

**Measures on the real line.** Measures on $(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{R})$ are defined by giving a **Stieltjes measure function** with the following properties:

i) $F$ is nondecreasing.

ii) $F$ is right continuous, i.e. $\lim_{y\downarrow x} F(y)=F(x)$.

:::

::: {#thm-2 name="Stieltjes Measures"}

Associated with each Stieltjes measure function $F$ there
is a unique measure $\mu$ on $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{R})$ with

$$
\mu((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

When $F(x) = x$ the resulting measure is called **Lebesgue measure**.

:::

::: {#cor-1 name="Generating the Borel σ-Field"}

Let $\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be the collection of **countable** open rectangles
of the form

$$
(a_1,b_1) \times \cdots \times (a_d,b_d),
$$

where the endpoints satisfy

$$
a_i,b_i \in \mathbb{Q} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}
$$

for $i = 1,\ldots,d$.

Then $\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ generates the Borel $\sigma$-field on $\mathbb{R}^d$; that is,

$$
\sigma\bigl(\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}^d)\bigr) = \mathcal{R}^d.
$$

:::

## Random Variables

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Measurable Map and Random Vector

A function $X : \Omega \to S$ is said to be a **measurable map** from $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ to $(S, \mathcal{S})$ if

$$
X^{-1}(B) \equiv \{\omega : X(\omega) \in B\} \in \mathcal{F}
$$

for all $B \in \mathcal{S}$.

If $(S, \mathcal{S}) = (\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{R}^d)$ and $d > 1$, then $X$ is called a **random vector**. Of course, if $d = 1$, $X$ is called a **random variable**.

We define $\sigma(X)$ to be the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ such that $X$ is measurable.

:::

::: {#thm-3 name="Measurability on a Generating Collection"}

Suppose $\mathcal{A}$ generates $\mathcal{S}$. If $X^{-1}(A) \in \mathcal{F}$ for every $A \in \mathcal{A}$, then $X$ is a measurable map from $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ to $(S, \mathcal{S})$.

:::

::: {#thm-4 name="Composition of Measurable Maps"}

If the maps

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to (S, \mathcal{S}), \\
f &: (S, \mathcal{S}) \to (T, \mathcal{T})
\end{aligned}
$$

are measurable, then $f(X)$ is a measurable map from $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ to $(T, \mathcal{T})$.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Why We Use the Borel $\sigma$-Field on $\mathbb{R}^d$

The Borel $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is the smallest $\sigma$-field that contains all open sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

An important property is that **every continuous function is Borel measurable**.

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Then, for every
$B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$,

$$
f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
$$

More generally, if $X$ is an $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued random vector and $f$ is continuous, then $f(X)$ is a random variable.

:::

## Distributions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Indicator Function

The **indicator function** of a set $A \in \mathcal{F}$:

$$
1_A(\omega) =
\begin{cases}
1, & \omega \in A, \\
0, & \omega \notin A.
\end{cases}
$$

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Distribution on $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{R})$

If $X$ is a random variable, then $X$ induces a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$, called its **distribution** by setting $\mu(A) = P(X \in A)$ for Borel sets $A$.
The right-hand side can be written
as $P(X^{-1}(A))$.

The distribution of a random variable $X$ is usually described by giving
its **distribution function**,

$$
F(x) = P(X \le x).
$$

:::

::: {#thm-5 name="Properties of Distribution Functions"}

Any distribution function $F$ has the following properties:

i) $F$ is nondecreasing.

ii) The limits at infinity are

    $$
    \lim_{x\to\infty} F(x) = 1,
    \qquad
    \lim_{x\to-\infty} F(x) = 0.
    $$

iii) $F$ is right continuous, i.e., $\lim_{y\downarrow x} F(y) = F(x)$.

iv) If $F(x-) = \lim_{y\uparrow x} F(y)$, then $F(x-) = P(X < x)$.

v) The probability at a point is

   $$
   P(X = x) = F(x) - F(x-).
   $$

:::

::: {#thm-6 name="Existence of a Distribution"}

If $F$ satisfies properties (i), (ii), and (iii), then $F$ is the distribution function of some random variable.

:::

## Integration

### Simple Functions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Simple Function

$\varphi$ is said to be a **simple function** if

$$
\varphi(\omega) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i 1_{A_i}
$$

and $A_i$ are disjoint sets with $\mu(A_i) < \infty$. If $\varphi$ is a simple function, we let

$$
\int \varphi \, d\mu = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i \mu(A_i).
$$

:::

::: {#thm-7 name="Properties of the Integral"}

$\varphi \ge \psi$ $\mu$-**almost everywhere** (or $\varphi \ge \psi$ $\mu$-a.e.) means

$$
\mu(\{\omega : \varphi(\omega) < \psi(\omega)\}) = 0.
$$

Let $\varphi$ and $\psi$ be simple functions.

i) **Nonnegativity.** If $\varphi \ge 0$ a.e., then $\int \varphi \, d\mu \ge 0$.

ii) **Homogeneity.** For any $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $\int a\varphi \, d\mu = a \int \varphi \, d\mu$.

iii) **Additivity.**

     $$
     \int (\varphi + \psi) \, d\mu
     = \int \varphi \, d\mu + \int \psi \, d\mu.
     $$

iv) **Monotonicity.** If $\varphi \le \psi$ a.e., then $\int \varphi \, d\mu \le \int \psi \, d\mu$.

v) **Equality almost everywhere.** If $\varphi = \psi$ a.e., then $\int \varphi \, d\mu = \int \psi \, d\mu$.

vi) **Triangle inequality.**

    $$
    \left|\int \varphi \, d\mu\right| \le \int |\varphi| \, d\mu.
    $$

:::

### Bounded Functions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Bounded Function

Let $E$ be a set with $\mu(E) < \infty$ and let $f$ be a bounded function that
vanishes on $E^c$.

To define the integral of $f$, we observe that if $\varphi, \psi$ are simple
functions that have $\varphi \le f \le \psi$, then we want to have

$$
\int \varphi \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu \le \int \psi \, d\mu,
$$

so we let

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int f \, d\mu
&= \sup_{\varphi \le f} \int \varphi \, d\mu \\
&= \inf_{\psi \ge f} \int \psi \, d\mu.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {#cor-2 name="Properties of the Integral for Bounded Functions"}

Let $E$ be a set with $\mu(E) < \infty$. If $f$ and $g$ are bounded functions that vanish on $E^c$, then:

i) **Nonnegativity.** If $f \ge 0$ a.e., then $\int f \, d\mu \ge 0$.

ii) **Homogeneity.** For any $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $\int af \, d\mu = a \int f \, d\mu$.

iii) **Additivity.**

     $$
     \int (f + g) \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu.
     $$

iv) **Monotonicity.** If $g \le f$ a.e., then $\int g \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu$.

v) **Equality almost everywhere.** If $g = f$ a.e., then $\int g \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu$.

vi) **Triangle inequality.**

    $$
    \left|\int f \, d\mu\right| \le \int |f| \, d\mu.
    $$

:::

### Nonnegative Functions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Nonnegative Function

For $f\ge 0$, define

$$
\int f\,d\mu = \sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_f}\int h\,d\mu,
$$

where $\mathcal{H}_f$ consists of bounded functions $h$ such that

$$
0 \le h \le f,
\qquad
\mu(\{x : h(x) > 0\}) < \infty.
$$

:::

::: {#lem-1 name="Approximation by Truncation"}

Let $E_n \uparrow \Omega$ have $\mu(E_n) < \infty$ and let $a \wedge b = \min(a,b)$. Then

$$
\int_{E_n} f \wedge n\, d\mu
\uparrow
\int f\, d\mu
\qquad \text{as } n \uparrow \infty.
$$

:::

::: {#cor-3 name="Properties of the Integral for Nonnegative Functions"}

Suppose $f,g \ge 0$.

i) **Nonnegativity.** $\int f \, d\mu \ge 0$.

ii) **Homogeneity.** If $a > 0$, then $\int af \, d\mu = a \int f \, d\mu$.

iii) **Additivity.**

     $$
     \int (f + g) \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu.
     $$

iv) **Monotonicity.** If $0 \le g \le f$ a.e., then $\int g \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu$.

v) **Equality almost everywhere.** If $0 \le g = f$ a.e., then $\int g \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu$.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## The Standard Definition of the Lebesgue Integral

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. For a nonnegative measurable
function $f:X\to[0,\infty]$, define

$$
\int_X f \, d\mu
= \sup_{\substack{s\text{ nonnegative simple} \\ s \le f}}
  \int_X s \, d\mu.
$$

In other words, approximate $f$ from below using nonnegative simple functions
and take the supremum of their integrals. The integral is allowed to equal
$+\infty$.

:::

### General Functions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## General Function

We say $f$ is integrable if

$$
\int |f|\,d\mu < \infty.
$$

The **positive and negative parts** of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^+(x) &= f(x)\vee 0, \\
f^-(x) &= (-f(x))\vee 0,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $a\vee b=\max(a,b)$. They satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= f^+(x)-f^-(x), \\
|f(x)| &= f^+(x)+f^-(x).
\end{aligned}
$$

We define the integral of $f$ by

$$
\int f \, d\mu = \int f^+ \, d\mu - \int f^- \, d\mu.
$$

:::

::: {#lem-2 name="Integral of a Difference"}

If $f=f_1-f_2$, where $f_1,f_2\ge 0$ and $\int f_i\,d\mu<\infty$ for $i=1,2$, then

$$
\int f\,d\mu = \int f_1\,d\mu - \int f_2\,d\mu.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-8 name="Properties of the Integral for General Functions"}

Suppose $f$ and $g$ are integrable.

i) **Nonnegativity.** If $f \ge 0$ a.e., then $\int f \, d\mu \ge 0$.

ii) **Homogeneity.** For all $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $\int af \, d\mu = a \int f \, d\mu$.

iii) **Additivity.**

     $$
     \int (f + g) \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu + \int g \, d\mu.
     $$

iv) **Monotonicity.** If $g \le f$ a.e., then $\int g \, d\mu \le \int f \, d\mu$.

v) **Equality almost everywhere.** If $g = f$ a.e., then $\int g \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu$.

vi) **Triangle inequality.**

    $$
    \left|\int f \, d\mu\right| \le \int |f| \, d\mu.
    $$

:::

### Notation for Special Cases

The notation for an integral depends on the underlying measure:

**Lebesgue measure.** For $\lambda$ on $(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{R}^d)$,

$$
\int f(x) \, dx = \int f \, d\lambda.
$$

**Lebesgue measure on an interval.** For $E = [a,b] \subset \mathbb{R}$,

$$
\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \int_E f \, d\lambda.
$$

**Stieltjes measure.** For $\mu$ on $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{R})$, with
$\mu((a,b]) = G(b) - G(a)$ for $a < b$,

$$
\int f(x) \, dG(x) = \int f \, d\mu.
$$

**Counting measure.** For a countable set $\Omega$, with $\mathcal{F}$
containing all subsets,

$$
\sum_{i \in \Omega} f(i) = \int f \, d\mu.
$$

## Properties of the Integral

### Radon–Nikodym Derivatives

::: {#thm-9 name="Radon–Nikodym Theorem"}

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be **$\sigma$-finite measures** on the same measurable space $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. If

$$
\nu\ll\mu,
$$

meaning

$$
\mu(A)=0\implies\nu(A)=0,
$$

then there exists a nonnegative measurable function $f$ such that

$$
\nu(A)=\int_A f\,d\mu
$$

for every $A\in\mathcal F$.

The function $f$ is unique **up to a $\mu$-null set** and is called the **Radon–Nikodym derivative**:

$$
f=\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}.
$$

:::

### Integral Inequalities

::: {#thm-10 name="Jensen's Inequality"}

Suppose $\varphi$ is convex, that is,

$$
\lambda\varphi(x) + (1-\lambda)\varphi(y)
\ge
\varphi\bigl(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y\bigr)
$$

for all $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$. If $\mu$ is a probability measure, and $f$ and $\varphi(f)$ are integrable, then

$$
\varphi\left(\int f \, d\mu\right)
\le
\int \varphi(f) \, d\mu.
$$

:::

For $1 \le p < \infty$, let

$$
\|f\|_p = \left(\int |f|^p \, d\mu\right)^{1/p}.
$$

Notice that $\|cf\|_p = |c| \cdot \|f\|_p$ for any real number $c$.

::: {#thm-11 name="Hölder's Inequality"}

If $p,q \in (1,\infty)$ with

$$
\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1,
$$

then

$$
\int |fg| \, d\mu \le \|f\|_p \|g\|_q.
$$

:::

::: {#cor-4 name="Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality"}

If $p=q=2$, then Hölder's inequality becomes the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality:

$$
\int |fg| \, d\mu \le \|f\|_2 \|g\|_2.
$$

:::

### Convergence Theorems

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Convergence in Measure and Almost Everywhere

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, and let
$f_n,f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable functions.

**Convergence in measure.** We say that $f_n \to f$ in measure if, for any
$\epsilon > 0$,

$$
\mu\bigl(\{x : |f_n(x)-f(x)| > \epsilon\}\bigr) \to 0
$$

as $n \to \infty$.

**Almost-everywhere convergence.** We say that $f_n$ converges to $f$ almost
everywhere if there exists a measurable set $Z\subseteq X$ with $\mu(Z)=0$ such that

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)=f(x)
$$

for every $x\in X\setminus Z$.

We write

$$
f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.e.}}f.
$$

On a space of finite measure, convergence in measure is a weaker assumption than
convergence a.e., but the next result is easier to prove in this greater generality.

:::

::: {#thm-12 name="Bounded Convergence Theorem"}

Let $E$ be a set with $\mu(E)<\infty$. Suppose $f_n$ vanishes on $E^c$, $|f_n(x)|\le M$, and $f_n\to f$ in measure. Then

$$
\int f \, d\mu = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int f_n \, d\mu.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-13 name="Fatou's Lemma"}

If $f_n \ge 0$ then

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu
\ge
\int\left(\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\right)\,d\mu.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-14 name="Monotone Convergence Theorem"}

If $f_n\ge0$ and $f_n\uparrow f$, then

$$
\int f_n\,d\mu \uparrow \int f\,d\mu.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-15 name="Dominated Convergence Theorem"}

If $f_n\to f$ a.e., $|f_n|\le g$ for all $n$, and $g$ is integrable, then

$$
\int f_n\,d\mu \longrightarrow \int f\,d\mu.
$$

:::
